NGSSS benchmarks (teacher-facing only - never on student pages)

Quarter 3 standards for this unit. Verify current wording at cpalms.org before quoting in formal documents.

  • VA.68.F.1.2 - Use innovative thinking to create or redesign a product, focusing on function and aesthetics.
  • VA.68.F.2.1 - Examine the careers and skills involved in producing and presenting art and design.
  • VA.68.S.3.4 - Use accurate art vocabulary to discuss media, techniques, and processes.
  • VA.68.C.1.4 - Use accurate art vocabulary to analyze the function and structure of artworks.
  • VA.68.O.3.1 - Use the structural elements of art and organizational principles to communicate an idea.
  • VA.68.H.3.3 - Examine the connection between technology and the visual arts and how each influences the other.
  • VA.68.C.2.3 - Use analytic skills to compare and contrast artworks across time and cultures.

Source grounding (anti-hallucination record)

FLAG: this unit has NO dedicated artwork source folder. This is a digital/AI concept unit ("transform a historical artwork through time"). There is no Unit-9 folder under 01_Analysis/Visual Art 2 Art Work. Per the build brief, ONE real public-domain historical artwork was selected from the available PD source folders to serve as the worked example of "a historical artwork you might reinterpret."   • Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889 A.D. - image viewed in this build at 01_Analysis/Visual Art 2 Art Work/Van gogh/Vincent van Gogh-StarryNight-Saint Remy, June 1889.jpg. Description (swirling deep-blue night sky; large yellow crescent moon upper right; bright haloed stars; long curling brushstrokes across the center; tall dark cypress tree on the left; small village with a thin church spire below low hills) written from the image. NGSSS benchmarks (teacher-facing only - never on student pages)

Source grounding (anti-hallucination record)

All artwork claims trace to images viewed in this build, plus the preserved 2025-26 course content. No dates or attributions were taken from memory. Each featured work below was opened and viewed with the Read tool from 01_Analysis/Visual Art 2 Art Work/Monet/.

  • Claude Monet, Impression, Sunrise, 1872 A.D. - viewed. A misty blue-green harbor at dawn; a small orange-red sun sits high, its reflection laid down as broken orange-red dashes on the water; loose, sketchy strokes; two small dark boats in front; faint ships and masts behind. Monet's signature and date appear at lower left. (Featured close-look image.)
  • Claude Monet, Haystacks (End of Summer), 1890-1891 A.D. - viewed. Two purple-brown haystacks in a lavender-blue field, warm gold-pink hills and trees behind, soft daylight. (Featured pair, version A.)
  • Claude Monet, Grainstack (Sunset), 1890-1891 A.D. - viewed (file Monet-HaystacksSunset-1890-1.jpg). One large haystack at right glowing red and violet against a blazing orange-yellow sky; thick, broken dabs of warm and cool color. (Featured pair, version B - shows the SAME subject under different light.)
  • Claude Monet, Blue Water Lilies, 1916-1919 A.D. - viewed. A nearly all-blue pond surface, vertical dark reed reflections, pale blue and white lily blossoms scattered across the water; very loose, woven strokes. (Supporting image, used by link or small.)
  • Claude Monet, Water Lily Pond, 1900 A.D. - viewed. A green Japanese-style footbridge over a pond crowded with lilies, willow leaves draping above; greens, reds, and touches of pink. (Supporting image.)

Note on titling: the file Monet-HaystacksSunset-1890-1.jpg is referred to on student pages as part of Monet's Haystacks / Grainstacks series. Both 1890-91 works are presented together to show how Monet painted the same subject under changing light.

Revision note (2026-07-14): Per teacher review ("use imagery for the folder, could be more clearer to view"), the Haystacks pair grid was widened from minmax(260px, 1fr) to minmax(340px, 1fr), and the Water Lily pair grid was widened from minmax(220px, 1fr) to minmax(320px, 1fr), so both image pairs render larger by default and Monet's broken-color brushwork stays visible instead of shrinking on narrower screens. The underlying image files were already the full-resolution files provided in the source folder; this was a display-size fix, not a re-source. VR removed course-wide (platform not yet finalized); its content is not reflected elsewhere since the module's Elements/Principles/close-look content already stands on its own.

  • Lichtenstein-MMaybe-1965.jpg - viewed. A blonde woman with a gloved hand to her head and a thought bubble reading "M-MAYBE HE BECAME ILL AND COULDN'T LEAVE THE STUDIO!" A later, more abstract double portrait of a woman (yellow hair, red lips, dotted face panel) and a man in a hat with a striped tie and a blue flower; angular Cubist-style fragments.   • Lichtenstein-StillLifeRed-1983.jpg - viewed. A still life: a white jar, a yellow scrolled cornice, window blinds, a small plant, and a coiled red rope on a yellow table; diagonal black hatching and Ben-Day dots; wood-grain frame edges. Not featured this cycle.

Now it is your turn to paint like an Impressionist. You will create an original landscape inspired by Monet, using short brushstrokes, layered color, and a clear sense of light. A bridge
A sunset landscape
A park scene
A flower field

Identify the foreground, middle ground, and background. The foreground is closest to you, the background is farthest away.

Foil Embossing

📋 PROJECT OVERVIEW
Now you build the design you planned last week. A foil embossing is a relief: you raise lines off a flat board, press shiny foil over them so the lines rise as real bumps, and then color the foil with bold, Fauvist color. The finished piece has texture you can feel and color that does not copy real life.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How can I combine raised texture and bold, non-realistic color in one relief artwork?
📋 WHAT YOU NEED
▶
A piece of cardboard for your base
▶
Yarn or string, and liquid glue
▶
Heavy-duty aluminum foil (thicker is sturdier)
▶
A glue stick
▶
Colored Sharpies or permanent markers
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Draw your free-form design on the cardboard, using the plan from your Module 15.01 Sketch. Keep the lines bold and simple.
2
Using liquid glue, trace over your lines and lay yarn along the wet glue. These raised lines become the texture you will feel through the foil.
3
Cut a piece of heavy-duty aluminum foil about an inch larger than your cardboard on each side. Heavy-duty foil is sturdier and less likely to rip.
4
Cover the back of the foil with a glue stick. Use plenty, and rub in one direction so the foil does not bunch up and tear. Lay it over your cardboard.
5
Take your time gently rubbing around each raised line. The more carefully you press the foil around the yarn, the more your design will rise up as relief.
6
Color the whole image with colored Sharpies, using bold, non-realistic Fauvist colors. Leave the raised lines uncolored so they shine and stand out.
7
Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist’s name.

It is signed, and the artist statement is filled in.

Write an exhibit label for each piece and place it beside its frame. Every label needs three things: the title of the piece, the medium it was made in (pencil, paint, collage, clay, and so on), and one sentence naming the Element of Art, Principle of Design, or technique it practiced.
6
Outline and color your frames, and glue or tape your photos or reproductions in place. Keep your sizes in proportion so no piece overpowers its neighbors.
7
Make it stand in 3D. Fold the bottom of the paper up to the floor line, then carefully cut along the vertical fold from the bottom edge up to the floor line so the two walls stand and form a corner. Glue it onto another sheet for the floor, add any finishing props, and sign your gallery as its curator.
📋 WHAT YOU NEED
▶
3 to 5 (or more) of your own finished artworks from earlier this year, or clear photos of them
▶
Two sheets of paper (one for the gallery, one for the floor), or a small box / cardboard
▶
A dark marker and any color you have (pencils, markers, or crayons)
▶
Small strips of paper for your exhibit labels
▶
Scissors and glue or tape
✏️ ARTIST STATEMENT (TYPE THIS IN THE SUBMISSION BOX)
In 2 to 3 sentences, in your own words, reflect on your growth across this whole year: What changed in your work between your earliest piece in this gallery and your most recent one? Which piece are you most proud of, and why? Which piece do you think best shows what you learned?
✅ WHAT MAKES A STRONG RETROSPECTIVE GALLERY
☐
It stands in 3D and displays 3 to 5 (or more) of your own finished artworks from earlier this year, each with a clear exhibit label (title, medium, and the Element/Principle or technique it practiced).
☐

☐

☐

☐

quizzes.title: Module 09.05 Short Quiz: Art Through Time
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: What does it mean to reinterpret a historical artwork?

answers.text: To trace it exactly so it looks identical
To use it as a starting point and remake it with new choices
To throw it away and start over with no connection to it
To sell a copy of it

questions.text: Which of these is the best description of how art styles changed through time?

answers.text: Styles never change; all art looks the same
Only the subject changes; the style always stays the same
Different eras paint similar subjects in different styles
Newer art is always better than older art

questions.text: You repaint a calm night scene using warm oranges and pinks instead of cool blues so it feels like a sunrise. Which choice are you using most to change the mood?
In this class, an AI image tool is best described as:

answers.text: A required step for every art project
The only correct way to reinterpret an artwork
A tool that decides your idea for you
One optional tool an artist may choose to use

questions.text:
When you reinterpret an artwork, you must keep everything exactly the same and are not allowed to change anything.

(A reinterpretation is built on deciding what to keep and what to change.)
Which set of words best names the choices an artist studies before reinterpreting a work?
Match each term to its meaning.

answers.right: Where things sit on the page and how the eye moves
The palette and the mood it creates
What the artwork shows: people, places, or objects
A new version that keeps some choices and changes others

quizzes.title: Module 10.05 Short Quiz: Impressionism and the Elements of Light
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: The Impressionists got their name from one of Claude Monet's paintings. Which painting was it?
What did Monet and the Impressionists most want to capture in a painting?

answers.text: A serious story from history or myth
A smooth surface with hidden brushstrokes
The way light looked in a single moment

questions.text: When an artist places small dabs of pure color side by side and lets the viewer's eye blend them, this is called:
Monet painted the same haystacks many times at different times of day. What does comparing the daylight version with the sunset version show us?

answers.text: He was bad at finishing a painting
Light and time of day completely change the colors and mood of a scene
He only liked the color orange

questions.text: Texture in an Impressionist painting comes from thick, short brushstrokes that you can almost feel on the surface.
In Impression, Sunrise, the sun's reflection is painted as a column of repeated orange dashes with a steady beat. Which Principle does that show best?
Match each art tool to the way Monet used it.

answers.right: Dabs of pure color placed side by side so the eye blends them
Short, thick brushstrokes that build a rough paint surface
Bright highlights against darker areas to show where light falls
Strokes that sweep and lead the eye across the scene

quizzes.title: Module 11.05 Short Quiz: Post-Impressionism (Van Gogh)
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: Post-Impressionism is a style that focused on which of the following?

answers.text: Copying nature as exactly as a photograph
Using only black, white, and gray
Personal expression, bold color, and dramatic brushstrokes

questions.text: Which artist is described in this lesson as one of the most important Post-Impressionist painters?
Impasto is a technique in which an artist does what?

answers.text: Paints with very thin, watery color
Lays paint on thick, so you can see the ridges and brush marks

questions.text: In The Starry Night, Van Gogh used swirling, same-direction brushstrokes to give the night sky a strong sense of movement.
How was Post-Impressionism different from the Impressionism that came before it?

answers.text: Impressionists used bolder color than Post-Impressionists
Post-Impressionists focused more on feeling and expression, not just capturing a quick moment
There was no difference between them

questions.text: In Wheatfield with Crows, the dark crows are what your eye goes to first. This focal point is an example of which Principle of Design?
Match each term to its meaning.

answers.right: Paint laid on thick, so you can see ridges and brush marks
How an artwork leads your eye to travel across it
A style built on personal feeling, bold color, and dramatic brushwork
An earlier style using light colors and loose strokes to catch a quick moment

quizzes.title: Module 12.05 Short Quiz: Primary Colors and Pop Art
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: Which list shows the three primary colors?
What makes the primary colors special?

answers.text: They are the only colors used in comic books
They cannot be made by mixing other colors together
They are always the brightest colors on the page
They were invented by Roy Lichtenstein

questions.text: Roy Lichtenstein became famous for making paintings that looked like what?
The rows of small, evenly spaced dots Lichtenstein painted to imitate comic-book printing are called what?
Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound, such as BOOM, POW, or ZAP.
Besides primary colors, which feature gives Lichtenstein's shapes their strong, clear comic-book look?
Match each term or work to its description.

answers.right: Red, yellow, and blue; cannot be mixed from other colors
Small evenly spaced dots that imitate comic-book printing
A word that imitates a sound, like POW or SPLASH
Two-panel painting of a fighter jet firing a rocket into an explosion; Tate, London
Painting of a woman with a thought bubble, red Ben-Day dots on her skin; Museum Ludwig, Cologne

quizzes.title: Module 13.05 Short Quiz: Color Theory and the Color Wheel
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: Which list shows the three primary colors?
What is a secondary color?

answers.text: A color you cannot mix from any other paints
A color made by mixing two primary colors
A color made by adding white to a primary
Another word for a warm color

questions.text: Which two primary colors mix to make orange?
On the color wheel, where does the secondary color green sit?
Warm colors are the reds, oranges, and yellows, and they tend to feel close and full of energy.
Which group lists only cool colors?
Match each color to whether it is primary or secondary.

answers.right: Primary
Secondary
Primary
Secondary

quizzes.title: Module 14.05 Short Quiz: Surrealism and Magritte
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: Surrealism is an art movement that explores what?

answers.text: Exact, photo-like copies of real life
Only the seven Elements of Art
Dreams, the imagination, and the hidden parts of the mind
Pictures of famous battles and kings

questions.text: René Magritte was a painter from which country?
Which sentence best describes how Magritte painted his strange ideas?

answers.text: With messy, blurry strokes so nothing is clear
Using only black and white, with no detail
Calm and realistic, so impossible scenes look believable

questions.text: In Magritte's Time Transfixed (1938 A.D.), now held by the Art Institute of Chicago, what comes out of the fireplace?
A common Surrealist move is to take an ordinary object and change one rule about it, such as its size, its place, or the world around it.
In Personal Values (1952 A.D.), now held by the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Magritte makes everyday grooming objects feel dreamlike mainly by doing what?

answers.text: Making them huge, with sky and clouds on the bedroom walls

questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

answers.right: An art movement that explores dreams and the imagination
A Belgian painter known for ordinary objects in strange settings
Feeling familiar but strange, the way a dream does
The part of a scene that is closest to the viewer

quizzes.title: Module 15.05 Short Quiz: Fauvism, Color, and Relief
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: The word Fauvism comes from the French word fauves. What does fauves mean?
Which phrase best describes the color in Fauvist painting?

answers.text: Realistic colors that copy nature exactly
Bold, non-realistic colors chosen for feeling
Colors that are always dull and faded

questions.text: Who was the leader of the Fauvism movement?
In Woman with a Hat (1905 A.D.), Matisse painted the woman’s face with unrealistic colors like green, yellow, and pink instead of realistic skin tones.
Which Element of Art describes how a surface feels, or looks like it would feel?
A relief is best described as an artwork that has...

answers.text: raised parts that stand up off a flat surface
no shapes or lines at all

questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

answers.right: An art movement using bold, non-realistic color
How a surface feels, or looks like it would feel
Artwork with raised parts that rise off the surface
The French artist who led the Fauves

quizzes.title: Module 16.05 Short Quiz: Expressionism and Edvard Munch
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: What is the main goal of Expressionism?

answers.text: To copy exactly what the eye sees
To show how something feels, not exactly how it looks
To use only black and white

questions.text: Edvard Munch was an artist from which country?
In The Scream, the sky and water are full of wavy lines that seem to move. Which Expressionist tool is that?
Munch stretches and bends the front figure so it looks the way panic feels. This choice is called what?
Munch chose the bright red and orange sky in The Scream to make the scene feel uneasy, not to copy a real sky.
When an artist picks a color for how it feels rather than how a real object looks, that artist is using what?
Match each term to its meaning.

answers.right: A style that shows feelings instead of an exact, realistic copy
Wavy, swirling lines that look like they are moving
Colors chosen for how they feel, not how things really look
Stretching or bending a figure or scene to show a feeling

quizzes.title: Module 17.05 Short Quiz: 3D Form & Exhibit Design
quizzes.description: 7 auto-graded questions on this module's key ideas and vocabulary.

questions.text: A sculpture has depth and you can walk all the way around it. What makes a sculpture different from a flat drawing?

answers.text: A drawing uses color and a sculpture never does
A drawing is three-dimensional and a sculpture is two-dimensional
A sculpture is three-dimensional (it has depth), while a drawing is two-dimensional (flat)
There is no difference between them

questions.text: In art, a flat area is a shape, but a 3D object with depth is called a what?
A curator leaves comfortable gaps of empty room between the pieces so visitors can step back and look. Which idea is the curator using on purpose?
In a gallery, five pieces are crowded on one wall and the other walls are bare. The room feels lopsided. Which Principle does the curator need to fix?
Giving every piece in a show the same frame style is one way a curator creates unity, the sense that the works belong together.
A curator places one tiny artwork alone on a huge wall, so it looks lost. Which Principle is out of adjustment?
Match each exhibit-design idea to what a curator does with it.

answers.right: Arranges 3D objects you can walk around, like sculptures and stands
Leaves room to walk and gaps between pieces
Repeats a color, frame, or theme so the show feels like one collection
Keeps each piece a sensible size next to its neighbors and the room

discussions.title: Module 09.03 Discussion Board: Remix It
discussions.html:
If you remixed The Starry Night by Vincent van Gogh for today, what would you change? Think about subject, colors, setting, or making it digital. Describe your remix in 2-3 sentences and explain what you would keep from the original.

Then answer this: How would you turn a famous painting into a digital artwork? What would a computer do well, and what does a human do better? (You do not need to use any AI tool to answer.)

Reply to 2 classmates: What part of their remix would you most like to see? Add one idea to make it even better.

discussions.title: Module 10.03 Discussion Board: Monet's Water Lilies
discussions.html:
See, Think, Wonder. Look at Blue Water Lilies by Claude Monet, from the water-lily series in this module's Instructional Page. Focus on color and brushstrokes. In your post, share:

I see... 2 things you notice in the artwork, such as a color you see or the way the brushstrokes look.

I think... what you think is going on, or what the artist was trying to show.

I wonder... 1 question you still have.

Reply to 2 classmates: Answer one of their "I wonder" questions, or share a different idea about what's going on.

discussions.title: Module 11.03 Discussion Board: Monet or Van Gogh?
discussions.html:
Look at Claude Monet's Impression, Sunrise (from Module 10) and Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night. Which one do you connect with more? Explain your choice using at least one art vocabulary word, and name one way the two artworks are alike. In your post, also compare their brushstrokes and use of color.

Reply to 2 classmates: Did they pick the same one as you? Share a reason they didn't mention.

discussions.title: Module 12.03 Discussion Board: Remix It: Whaam! in Pop Art Style
discussions.html:
If you remixed Whaam! by Roy Lichtenstein for today, what would you change? Think about subject, colors, setting, or making it digital. Try remixing an everyday object or a comic panel in Pop Art style, and focus on pattern: where would you use Ben-Day dots? Describe your remix in 2-3 sentences and explain what you would keep from the original. Look at Whaam! again here: Whaam! at Tate.

Reply to 2 classmates: What part of their remix would you most like to see? Add one idea to make it even better.

discussions.title: Module 13.03 Discussion Board: Warm, Cool, or Complementary
discussions.html:
Choose one artwork from an earlier module: Impression, Sunrise by Claude Monet (Module 10) or The Starry Night by Vincent van Gogh (Module 9).

Find one Element of Art and one Principle of Design in your artwork. For the Element, use color: find warm and cool colors, or find complementary colors (colors across from each other on the color wheel). For each one, tell: - where you see it in the artwork - why you think the artist used it

Reply to 2 classmates: Did they find something you missed? Agree or disagree, and explain why.

discussions.title: Module 14.03 Discussion Board: Interview Magritte
discussions.html:
Look at The Son of Man (1964) by René Magritte, the man with the apple in front of his face: The Son of Man.

If you could interview René Magritte, what 2 questions would you ask? Make at least one of your questions about The Son of Man. Then choose one question and guess how the artist might answer, using what you learned this module.

Reply to 2 classmates: Pick one of their questions and give your own guess at the answer.

discussions.title: Module 15.03 Discussion Board: See, Think, Wonder: Matisse's Snail
discussions.html:
Look at The Snail (1953) by Henri Matisse. In his later years, Matisse made art by cutting shapes from painted paper. As you look, focus on shape and color.

In your post, share:

  • I see... 2 things you notice in the artwork.
  • I think... what you think is going on, or what the artist was trying to show.
  • I wonder... 1 question you still have.

Reply to 2 classmates: Answer one of their "I wonder" questions, or share a different idea about what's going on.

discussions.title: Module 16.03 Discussion Board: Line and Color in The Scream
discussions.html:
Find one Element of Art and one Principle of Design in The Scream by Edvard Munch. For the Element, choose line or color. For each one, tell:

  • Where you see it in the artwork.
  • Why you think the artist used it. How does it show emotion?

You can discuss the feelings in the artwork without sharing anything personal you are not comfortable sharing.

Reply to 2 classmates: Did they find something you missed? Agree or disagree, and explain why.

discussions.title: Module 17.03 Discussion Board: Gallery Walk: Two Stars and a Wish
discussions.html:
Post a photo of your finished 3D mini gallery. Write 1-2 sentences about one design choice you made and how it connects to an artist or movement from this year whose influence shows in your gallery. Name the artist or movement.

When you reply, use this format:

  • Two Stars: Two things that work well, using art vocabulary.
  • A Wish: One kind suggestion or idea.

Reply to 2 classmates: Use the Two Stars and a Wish format above.
